questions.prompt: This footwear is shown on the Lab 1 safety slide. Why is it not allowed in micro lab?

options.text: Shoes must be made of rubber so they can be bleached
Shoes must have closed toes and protect the tops of the feet
Only lab-issued shoe covers may be worn in micro lab
Sandals are allowed only when no liquid cultures are used

questions.explanation: Safe shoes: sturdy soles, closed toes, and protection for the tops of the feet.

why.A: No material rule — the rule is sturdy soles, closed toes, protected tops of feet.
why.C: Shoe covers aren't part of the lab safety policy.
why.D: Closed-toe shoes are required every lab, not just with liquids.

questions.prompt: What is the very first thing you do at your lab table, before setting anything down on it?

options.text: Set out your lab manual and notes
Disinfect the table
Wash your hands at the sink
Put on safety glasses from the UV cabinet

questions.explanation: Disinfect your table upon entering the lab — do not set any items down until it has been disinfected — and again at the end of lab.

why.A: Items must not be set down until the table has been disinfected.
why.C: Handwashing comes right after disinfecting tables, and is the last action before leaving.
why.D: Glasses are worn when instructed; disinfecting the table comes first.

questions.prompt: What is your LAST action before leaving micro lab?

options.text: Disinfecting the lab table
Storing safety glasses in the UV cabinet
Placing your plates in the collection tray
Washing your hands

questions.explanation: Wash hands immediately after disinfecting tables; washing hands is your last action before leaving lab.

why.A: You disinfect the table at the end of lab, then wash hands as the very last step.
why.B: Glasses are stored after use, but handwashing is the last action.
why.C: Cultures are put away before cleanup; washing hands comes last.

questions.prompt: After use, where are these stored?

options.text: In your lab drawer with your manual
In the UV cabinet, after being disinfected
In the biohazard bag after each lab
In the autoclave so they are sterilized

questions.explanation: Safety glasses: wear when instructed, disinfect before and after use, store in the UV cabinet.

why.A: Glasses are disinfected and stored in the UV cabinet, not with personal items.
why.C: Glasses are reused; only cultures/contaminated materials go into biohazard bags.
why.D: Glasses are disinfected before and after use and stored in the UV cabinet.

questions.prompt: This piece of equipment is used to sterilize your loop. What safety rule applies to it?

options.text: It must be cleaned with immersion oil after use
It must always be stored in the UV cabinet
It may only be used with liquid cultures
It gets very hot — unplug it when not in use

questions.explanation: Microincinerators and hot plates get very hot — be careful and always unplug hot things when not in use.

why.A: Oil cleanup applies to microscopes, not the microincinerator.
why.B: The UV cabinet is for safety glasses.
why.C: It sterilizes loops for any culture; the rule is about heat.

questions.prompt: Where do used cultures and contaminated materials (like a used swab) go?

options.text: Into the regular trash can
Into the biohazard bag
Into the sink, followed by bleach
Back into the collection tray

questions.explanation: Disposal of cultures/contaminated materials: always into the biohazard bags. Used test tubes go in the designated location.

why.A: Trash cans are for other, non-contaminated materials only.
why.C: Cultures are never poured down the sink; they go in biohazard bags.
why.D: The collection tray is for plates being incubated, not waste.

questions.prompt: You knock over a tube and it breaks. What should you do?

options.text: Sweep up the glass yourself right away
Immediately report it to the instructor
Cover it with paper towels and keep working
Tell your tablemate so they can clean it

questions.explanation: Immediately report spills, broken glass or other accidents. Don't clean them yourself — and spills will not affect your grade.

why.A: Do NOT try to clean up spills or broken glass yourself.
why.C: Accidents must be reported and cleaned using proper safety protocols.
why.D: Spills are cleaned per protocol by/with the instructor, not hidden or delegated.

questions.prompt: Which biosafety level of organisms is used in this micro lab?

options.text: BSL-2
BSL-3
BSL-4
BSL-1

questions.explanation: Only Biosafety Level 1 organisms are used; probiotic strains are used whenever possible.

why.A: The lab uses only BSL-1 organisms, which health authorities classify as safe for most people.
why.B: BSL-3 organisms are not used in teaching labs like this one.
why.C: BSL-4 organisms are the most dangerous; they are never used here.

questions.prompt: Liquid cultures must always be kept in a:

options.text: Biohazard bag
Beaker on your notes
Test tube rack
Coplin jar

questions.explanation: Cultures: always use test tube racks with liquid cultures and always use aseptic technique.

why.A: Biohazard bags are for disposal, not holding cultures you're using.
why.B: Cultures must never be placed on notes, manuals or binders.
why.D: Coplin jars hold staining reagents, not cultures.

questions.prompt: This organism (shown on the Microbe Spotlight slide) is a common resident of the human gut. What type of microbe is Escherichia coli?

options.text: A yeast (fungus)
A protozoan
A bacterium (prokaryote)
An archaeon

questions.explanation: E. coli is a bacterium. Under special circumstances it can cause UTIs, traveler's diarrhea, food poisoning, wound infections, sepsis or meningitis.

why.A: E. coli is a bacterium; Candida and Saccharomyces are the yeasts.
why.B: E. coli is prokaryotic; protozoa are eukaryotes.
why.D: E. coli is in Domain Bacteria, not Archaea.

questions.prompt: These purple oval cells are Candida albicans. Which condition can C. albicans overgrowth cause?

options.text: Farmer's lung
Traveler's diarrhea
Thrush
Mad cow disease

questions.explanation: C. albicans overgrowth can cause vaginal yeast infections, thrush, skin rashes, systemic infections and GI tract infections.

why.A: Farmer's lung is caused by Aspergillus spp.
why.B: Traveler's diarrhea is caused by certain E. coli strains.
why.D: Mad cow disease (BSE) is caused by prions.

questions.prompt: Farmer's lung, a respiratory hypersensitivity (allergic reaction), is caused by:

options.text: Candida albicans
Escherichia coli
Penicillium spp.
Aspergillus spp.

questions.explanation: Aspergillus spp. may cause farmer's lung (allergic reaction), aspergillosis (respiratory infection) and systemic infections.

why.A: Candida causes yeast infections, thrush, rashes, systemic and GI infections.
why.B: E. coli causes UTIs, diarrhea and food poisoning, not farmer's lung.
why.C: Penicillium isn't listed as causing farmer's lung.

questions.prompt: This is a helminth (a fluke). Why are helminths included in a micro course?

options.text: They are prokaryotes that share many traits with bacteria and archaea
They are acellular agents that replicate only inside host cells
They are officially classified as microbes in every textbook
Their larval stages are microscopic and they are highly relevant to human health

questions.explanation: Helminths are not considered microbes, but their larval stages are microscopic and they matter to human health.

why.A: Helminths are eukaryotes in Kingdom Animalia.

questions.prompt: What makes prions different from every other disease-causing agent covered in the course?

options.text: They are obligate intracellular parasites
They are acellular
They are surrounded by a lipid envelope
They do not possess genetic material

questions.explanation: Prions are proteinaceous infectious agents: misfolded proteins that cause other proteins to misfold. They lack genetic material.

why.A: Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites; that isn't unique to prions.
why.B: Viruses are also acellular, so that's not what sets prions apart.
why.C: Some viruses have envelopes; prions are just misfolded proteins.

questions.prompt: Which statement about viruses is FALSE?

options.text: They are acellular
They are obligate intracellular parasites
They have a DNA or RNA core in a protein coat (nucleocapsid)
Some have a lipid envelope around the nucleocapsid
They replicate on their own outside of host cells

questions.explanation: Viruses are replicated by the living host cell — they cannot replicate on their own.

why.B: True — they can only replicate inside a living host cell.
why.C: True — the core plus coat is the nucleocapsid.
